The DFS ecosystem's core structure is defined by two interlocking primitives: the research packet hierarchy and the optimizer slate kernel. The former enforces a temporal lattice of knowledge, while the latter defines a constrained optimization landscape. These interact through a temporal rule that ensures all new data enters the system in a causally consistent manner. The failure mode of the hierarchy occurs when outdated or untimestamped research corrupts the lattice. The kernel breaks down when the slate size exceeds computational bounds. Dualities emerge in how these structures mirror each other: the research packet is a static snapshot of a dynamic process, while the slate is a dynamic constraint on a static set of players. The system's robustness depends on maintaining a strict separation between these layers, preventing cross-layer contamination.
